articles.title: Act for Nutrition conference: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries
articles.description: A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis. With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations. View the full agenda here . 11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region. “We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box ... the British decided to give self-rule,” he said. He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things. 11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun. 11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform. “It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”. “We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted. Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”. He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition. “The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said. 11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’ Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow. “Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said. 11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia in South Asia were advocacy for policy engagement. She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”. Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition. “This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added. Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries. “Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said. The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.” She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”. 11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone. “Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said. “Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said. 11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition. “Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty ... are affecting food and health systems,” he said. He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience. “Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems. 10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins The session on global and regional realities has now begun. 10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting. “Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said. She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes. “Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said. ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’ Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”. “When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said. She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases. 10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations. “When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required. 10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food. “It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said. World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity. “Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action. 10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today. “It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said. “We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action. “Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said. 10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity “Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. “Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues. “90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said. “If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said. “That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said. 9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority. He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development. “We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said. “Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said. 9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either. “You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said. “With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said. “That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added. Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”. “We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said. “So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added. She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”. 9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’ In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted. “These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said. “And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said. 9:45am - Conference begins The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran. Attendees of the Act For Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

articles.title: Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see | Devi Sridhar
articles.description: You could be walking around symptom-free and not know you’re pre-diabetic, living with hypertension or at a high risk of a heart attack Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” Benjamin Franklin’s adage goes. Yet that simple prescription has been hard to follow in the current NHS. As has been frequently highlighted , one of the biggest challenges for the health system is not just how much we spend per capita, but where and when it is spent. In England, there has been an ongoing shift within the NHS budget towards acute hospital care – treating people in hospitals, often after they are already quite ill – while funding for primary care such as GPs has fallen. The consequence is that the NHS is increasingly paying for serious and expensive disease treatment, rather than investing upstream to prevent disease in the first place. We spend heavily on dealing with heart attacks, strokes and other life-threatening conditions, rather than identifying those who are at higher risk and intervening earlier to reduce their chances of getting ill. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.title: Anal aftercare 101: Expert tips on taking care of your partner after bottoming
articles.description: It’s easy to get so focused on the pleasure sex brings that you don’t think about what comes afterward, but whether it’s cuddling, a warm bath, or pillow talk, aftercare should be part of your post-sex routine — especially if you’re into anal sex . You may think that aftercare is just for kinky sex , but even the most vanilla among us can benefit, and if you’re regularly topping , you should be putting effort into taking extra care of your partner after anal sex. The goal of anal aftercare is to return to equilibrium, transition back into the real world after intense sex, and care for a body that may have been put through the wringer. “Aftercare is what you do in the aftermath of sex to maximize care and wellbeing,” Good Vibes Sexologist Carol Queen tells Out . “There is a solo version of this, but the term is particularly used to refer to checking with a sex/play partner about how they are feeling: seeing if they're doing well, communicating about your scene or date, finding out whether they need anything from you.” Bottoming on its own can be a particularly vulnerable and physically taxing sex act, so even if you’re not in a Dom/sub relationship or into kinky sex, anal aftercare should become part of your postcoital regimen. What is anal aftercare? In its simplest form, anal aftercare is a term to describe the way you care for your partner after anal sex, especially for the receptive partner. “It’s about what everyone’s mind and body may prefer or need after a round of anal,” says Todd Baratz, an AASECT-certified sex therapist at #LUBELIFE . “It’s really no different from sex aftercare — or any kind of care— it just happens to describe the period specifically after anal sex.” Just like the kind of aftercare that kinksters have made a required part of BDSM sex, anal aftercare is about looking after your partner’s emotional wellbeing and the impact of any kind of anal play, like “toy play, anal intercourse, digital penetration, fisting, enema play and so on,” Queen says. “Not all anal play necessarily fits into the kink category, though certainly some does, and there are plenty of people who would view all anal as kinky,” Queen says. “But any anal play comes with taboos that might still be felt by either partner; and additionally, anal, like some forms of BDSM, can result in pain or damage if it isn't done properly and with care. Even when you've had a perfect anal experience, there still might be a history of painful or even abusive or coercive anal behavior, which means emotion and reaction can run high with this kind of sex.” Why is aftercare important after anal sex? Whether you’ve just hooked up for the first time and don’t plan a repeat or you’ve topped a long-term partner, you should still be thinking about anal aftercare and how you can make the experience better for the person you’re sleeping with. Not only will this show your partner that you care about what happens to their body and emotions post sex, but “thinking about your partner's experience and well-being is how you get better at having sex,” Queen says. “Another function of aftercare is to express caring,” she says. “Even if it's a one-time sexual experience, a person can feel more valued and respected, and is less likely to feel used, with aftercare, where their partner (temporary or long-term) is supportive of them and helps them deal with any aftermath of the experience. It can be equally meaningful for the top, relationally speaking.” And if you’re not prepared to do that, Queen suggests sticking to solo play and buying a sex doll instead. “Because they're a human being who is due respect and care; they're only a fuckpuppet if you negotiate it,” she says. “A person who doesn't feel the ability to take their partner's experience into account might want to invest in a nice sex doll.” Baratz agrees and says that taking care of your partner after you’ve penetrated their body during anal sex should be a given. “We could ask, ‘Why is care important?’ and the answer would seem obvious, but for some reason people approach sex as a separate category,” he says. “Sex, cuddling, cooking, walking around together — all of these can be thought about similarly in terms of the care we want to show ourselves and our partners. Sex in particular can be a vulnerable experience physically, emotionally, and relationally, so we need to be intentional about the care we show ourselves and our partners afterward.” What should you do before you even start having anal sex? Before you ever get to the aftercare, there are plenty of things you can do to reduce the physical impact of anal sex and bottoming. Unlike some other forms of sex, anal play can cause pain, discomfort, or even damage, but luckily there is plenty you can do to help prevent this so that your aftercare can be more focused on emotional and physical comfort than dealing with a newly formed anal fissure or other tissue damage. If you want to reduce any pain and discomfort during or post-anal sex, you’ll need to prep your body first. “Make sure that as a receptive partner you’re paying attention to pain and not trying to push through it,” Baratz says. “Make sure you’re relaxed before receiving penetration. Sometimes it can be helpful to use plugs, dilators, or dildos (also with a lot of lube) before starting to have anal sex. Stop whenever you need to and take breaks. If you’re paying attention to all of this during sex, you’re much more likely to feel good afterward.” And you can never have enough lube, according to Baratz, who says, “If you’re worried about making a mess, put down a towel, a tarp, whatever you need, but nothing should limit the amount of lube you use. It’s for both safety and pleasure.” Leading anal surgeon Dr. Evan Goldstein , who owns Bespoke Surgical and now has his own line of anal sex prep products available at CVS , says that not over-douching, stretching your body slowly with a dilator set when you’re on your own, and focusing on foreplay and pre-dilation with your partner during sex will all help you avoid injury. “All it takes is one mishap to potentially lead you down the road toward a chronic anal issue,” he says. “Bottoming is a sport, and practice makes perfect. I always say you can be submissive and still be in control. That control comes from the preparatory routines above.” You also don’t want to overdo it when it comes to the number of times you bottom back to back. “My partner, also a sexologist, and I were once talking to his anal doc and he told us almost all the rectal tears they saw at the hospital nearest the Castro were people who tried to play all weekend,” Queen warns. “Overdoing it with anal can not only cause pain, it can cause life-threatening injury.” 10 anal aftercare tips Anal aftercare is going to look different depending on the person you slept with and what their needs are post hook-up, but the experts have some tried and true tips to help you take care of your partner’s emotional and physical wellbeing after any kind of anal play. 1. Talk about aftercare beforehand According to Baratz, the best time to have a conversation about what you want aftercare to look like should start before you have sex so that you can “talk about sexual preferences, including your wishes for aftercare. Discuss what that includes or could include.” 2. Pillow talk When you both are coming down from an intense sexual experience, take the time to talk openly with your partner. “What I often try educating my clients about is aftercare isn't just physical – my happiest and healthiest patients also check in mentally, not only with themselves, but also their partners,” Goldstein says. “Something as simple as asking how they're feeling, what worked, what didn’t, etc. This tells them you're paying attention, and it also gives soreness a chance to get addressed early so that you can set yourself up for success next time.” Baratz agrees and says you should consider this time to do a sexual recap. Sexual recap and ask your partner, “What felt good? What did you like? What would you want to try next time?” 3. Cuddle time Physical touch can be incredibly helpful for everyone’s emotional well-being after anal sex, but especially for whoever bottomed. “Stay in contact with your partner physically—hold them or touch them—as they ‘come down’ from the experience,” Queen says. And don’t rush the process, try to stay present with your partner “Physically, staying close also helps — cuddling, a warm shower together, just quiet time before jumping back into the rest of the day,” Goldstein says. “The nervous system needs time to come down off that level of tension, and having a partner who isn't rushing that process makes a real difference.” 4. How does your body feel? Don’t forget to advocate for yourself. It may make you feel vulnerable, but it’s important to tell your partner what you need from them. “Pay attention to your body and what you need, while also asking your partner if they need anything. And share if there’s something you want or need,” Baratz says. 5. Ask what they need After anal sex, your partner will need to hydrate, maybe have a snack, or take a warm Epsom salt bath. This is something you can discuss ahead of time and then get it prepared so that they don’t have to think about it. “Ask them what they need: water, a bit of food, a warm washcloth, bath or shower,” Queen says. “Get or prepare that for them.” 6. Keep an eye on bleeding After anal sex, you’re going to want to monitor any bleeding that occurs, especially for more intense acts like anal fisting. ”Make sure any bleeding is minor or temporary,” Queen says. “That means it isn't copious and continuing to bleed, but stops shortly after play. If blood continues to drip and doesn't stop, accompany them to urgent care or the ER.” 7. Help clean up While your partner is resting, it’s a good time to take care of any mess that the two of you made. “If you were playing with toys, gather them up and get them ready to clean,” Queen says. 8. Don’t leave right away Even if this is a one-night stand or a quick hookup, don’t sneak out. Stick around to provide aftercare and don’t ditch them until they’re feeling emotionally stable. “Don’t leave before they're ready to be left alone — that is, if you don't live with them or have plans to stay,” Queen says. 9. Take constructive criticism When you’re having your post anal sex check in, take what you partner says to heart and incorporate it next time so you can really rock their world. “Some partners will welcome a chance to share feedback about the play itself; this can help you learn more about your partner and about how to give better anal pleasure,” Queen says. 10. Check in later Anal aftercare doesn’t end when you say goodbye. Touch base a couple days later to make sure they aren’t having any lingering pain or need anything from you emotionally. “A day or so later, call or meet to check in and see how they're doing,” Queen says. What kind of anal aftercare should you do for yourself? If you slept with a selfish partner who didn’t stick around after their orgasm — we’ve all been there — or you just like to provide yourself a little self-care, there are things you can do to take care of your own bottom after bottoming. Right after, skip the scented wipes and instead use a gentle external wash to help remove lube so you don’t irritate already-sensitive tissue, and don’t feel like you have to douche. “If there's soreness or swelling, a nice, warm Epsom salt bath does a lot of work relaxing the pelvic floor and the skin,” Goldstein says. “A lightweight, quick-drying cream or a calming suppository can help too, and ibuprofen is fine for inflammation. I'd steer people away from numbing agents like lidocaine — they mask the problem instead of helping it, and they can also inflame the tissue further.” Over the course of the next few days, you’ll want to support your body’s natural ability to heal by staying hydrated and taking a daily fiber supplement and synbiotic to keep your stool soft so you don’t strain, since “straining is one of the most common things that turns mild soreness into something worse like a fissure or a hemorrhoid,” Goldstein says. “Breathe normally during bowel movements instead of holding your breath,” he recommends. “And give the area a break — that means holding off on more sex until soreness has fully resolved. If sessions were longer or more intense, that recovery window should stretch out too. Watch for warning signs — worsening pain, swelling, discharge, bleeding beyond light spotting, fever — that's when I recommend booking an appointment to see your doctor."
